lines.text: A small green island that France and Britain fought over again and again, and that gave the world two Nobel laureates. This is the story of Saint Lucia.
In 1650 French settlers came to the island, and in time Castries, on its sheltered harbour, would become the capital.
The island changed hands many times. In 1782 a great naval battle was fought nearby, the Battle of the Saintes, between the British and French fleets.
Britain kept the island from 1814. In 1915 W. Arthur Lewis was born there. The economist would win the Nobel Prize in 1979.
John Compton, born in 1925, would lead Saint Lucia to independence as its first prime minister.
In 1930 Derek Walcott was born in Castries. His long poem Omeros sang of the island, and won him the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Philip J. Pierre was born in 1954, and became prime minister in 2021.
In 1979 Saint Lucia became independent, the same year Arthur Lewis won his Nobel Prize.
In 2001 Julien Alfred was born. At the Paris Olympics she won the hundred metres, the island's first Olympic medal.
And the twin volcanic spires of the Pitons, rising straight from the sea, were made a World Heritage Site in 2004.
Once fought over by empires, Saint Lucia now stands proudly as its own.
